---
title: "Spot the Mirage"
---

::: {.ao-story}
The maze walls shimmer. Some corridors are real, and some are Mirages: passages that look exactly right and lead nowhere, and your companion strides toward the nearest one without a doubt. A guide cannot tell them apart by their look, only by walking them. Learn what a false corridor looks like, and how to test one.
:::

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will recognise plausible-but-false output (a hallucination), and check it without asking the model that produced it.
- **Before you start:** [Where Machines Fail](../codon-mill/where-machines-fail.html), a terminal and Python.
- **Time:** about 10 minutes.
:::

## Plausible but false output

You will rely on agent output in analysis, so you need to know how it goes wrong. A language model produces text that *fits*. Sometimes it fits reality, and sometimes it only fits the pattern of what a correct answer would look like. The second kind is a **hallucination**. It reads smoothly, sounds confident, and is wrong. Confidence and detail tell you nothing about which kind you have.

Common hallucinations in analysis work:

- **Invented functions and flags**: a method or option that sounds right but does not exist. Try it: `"ATGCGC".reverse_complement()` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'reverse_complement'`.
- **Invented references**: a citation with a believable author, journal and DOI that points to nothing, or to a different paper.
- **Invented values and paths**: a plausible number, column name or file path that was never in your data.
- **Self-confirmation**: asking the same agent "are you sure?" often gets a fluent yes.

The cure is **checking against something the agent did not write**: run it, look it up, recompute it another way.

::: {.ao-lore}
## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Reduce hallucinations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it lists ways to make a model show its support (quote first, allow "I don't know"), the opposite of a confident mirage.
- [Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548): arXiv (ICLR 2024), paper. Why read: it shows assistants often agree with a user's stated view, which is why asking an agent "are you sure?" proves little.
- [On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173): ACL Anthology (ACL 2020), paper. Why read: it found invented content in every neural summary tested; the models are pre-chat-era, so read it for the direction, not current rates.
- [Best practices for Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it recommends giving the agent a way to verify its work, the habit this quest turns into a check you run yourself.
:::
